lesson.title: From Typed Commands to Saved Programs: Python Scripts
lesson.summary: A Python script is a text file of saved statements that the interpreter runs from top to bottom in one pass, which is what turns quick REPL experiments into real, reusable software.
lesson.body:
The REPL from the previous chapter is excellent for quick experiments, but it has an obvious limitation: everything you type disappears once you close the session. If you want to run the same set of steps again tomorrow, or share them with someone else, or have a computer run them automatically overnight, you need something more permanent. That something is a script, a plain text file, conventionally ending in the .py extension, that contains a full sequence of Python statements written out in order.

Running a script uses the exact same Python interpreter discussed two chapters ago, just given a whole file at once instead of a single line typed interactively. From a terminal, you would type a command like python temperature.py, and the interpreter reads the entire file, translates it, and executes every statement from the top of the file to the bottom, in order, exactly once, unless the code itself contains loops or function calls that repeat certain lines.

Consider a file named temperature.py containing:

celsius = 20
fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
print(fahrenheit)

Tracing this from top to bottom: the first line binds the name celsius to the integer value 20. The second line computes celsius * 9, which is 180, then divides by 5 using Python's true division operator, which always produces a decimal result, giving 36.0, then adds 32, giving 68.0, and binds that result to the name fahrenheit. The third line calls print on fahrenheit, so running python temperature.py displays 68.0. Notice that unlike the REPL, nothing is displayed automatically after the first two lines. Assignments never display anything on their own in a script, and even an expression by itself on a line would produce no visible output in a script, only an explicit call to print does.

Scripts matter because real software is rarely just one or two lines. A script can grow to hundreds or thousands of lines, be organized into reusable functions, be stored under version control so changes over time are tracked, and be shared with teammates or run automatically as part of a larger system, none of which is realistic to do inside a REPL session that vanishes when closed. A script file is also easy to edit and rerun as many times as needed, which matters once you are testing and refining logic rather than just checking one quick expression.

Most of the programs you write for the rest of this course, and essentially all real-world Python software, will take the form of scripts like this one rather than REPL sessions. Many programmers actually use both together in practice, drafting and testing a tricky piece of logic in the REPL first, where feedback is immediate, and then copying the working version into a script once it behaves correctly, so it can be saved and reused. The next chapter looks at comments, a way to leave notes inside a script for human readers without affecting what the interpreter actually executes.
